title: Simchat Torah
hookLine: the reading finishes Deuteronomy and begins Genesis on the same day, with dancing
carry: finish and begin the same day

lines: EVERY SCROLL OUT OF THE ARK.
cards: Picture the most serious room you know, a place of quiet prayer, at its loudest. Every Torah scroll is out of the ark.

People carry them in their arms like partners at a wedding, dancing in circles, singing, spilling into the street. Kids ride on shoulders waving flags. Someone's grandfather, who never dances, is dancing.
A scroll gets passed to someone who's never held one. The circles go around seven times, and nobody's in a hurry. This is the last day of the fall holidays.

teach.h: THE BRIDEGROOMS OF TORAH AND GENESIS.
teach.b: The day is called Simchat Torah, the joy of the Torah. It comes right after Sukkot: in Israel it's the same day as the festival called Shemini Atzeret; outside Israel it's the day after.

Back on day twenty you met the scroll that never stays finished: the last lines of Deuteronomy, ending "in the sight of all Israel," and then at once, from a second scroll, "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth."
Today it happens, and the readers get honors. Their titles: the bridegroom of the Torah and the bridegroom of Genesis, and in many communities today, brides too.
Then the dancing, the hakafot: seven circles around the reading table, every scroll in somebody's arms. Notice what nobody is doing. The scrolls stay closed, wrapped in their covers.

No one is reading, explaining or being tested. People often point out that on this one day, the great scholar and the child who can't read a word are equal: all anyone is doing is holding the Torah and dancing.

teach.h: THE CHILDREN UNDER ONE PRAYER SHAWL.
teach.b: In many synagogues all the children are called up together under one big prayer shawl, spread over them like a canopy. The dancing turned up in unexpected places.

teach.h: MOSCOW, THE 1960S: DANCING IN THE STREET.
teach.b: In the Soviet Union in the 1960s, when religious life was pressed down hard, thousands of young Jews gathered in the street outside the Moscow synagogue on Simchat Torah night, singing and dancing.
Many knew no Hebrew and none of the prayers. They knew the date. The writer Elie Wiesel went to see it and wrote about it in a book called The Jews of Silence.
The joy is in holding the book, not in having mastered it.

how: On Simchat Torah, synagogues take out all their Torah scrolls and dance with them in seven circuits called hakafot, read the end of Deuteronomy and the start of Genesis, and in many places call all the children up together under a prayer shawl.

games.q: you've just finished reading the whole Torah, a year's work. the congregation is celebrating. what happens next?
o: close the scroll and rest until next week.
read the last portion a second time.
games.why: a second scroll is opened and Genesis begins at once, so no one can say the Torah was finished and put away.

practice: Think of something you've finished recently, a project, a season, a chapter of your life, and let it be finished. Then ask what might begin right now, and hold the end and the beginning in the same breath.
Reread, or recall, the first line of something you love: a book, a song, a poem, a letter someone wrote you.

wordCard.voice: Simchat Torah. The joy of the Torah: the day the year's reading ends with Deuteronomy and begins again with Genesis, with dancing.
